newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa business mood perks up but no H1 rate cut.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa business mood perks up but no H1 rate cut.

text.p: Business confidence is on the rise, helped by a bullish budget last month, but interest rates are unlikely to be cut before mid-year, the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said on Tuesday.

"It looks as though we are in a rising phase of business confidence after the uncertainty caused by the instability of the rand last year," director of economic policy Ben van Rensburg told reporters.
Sacob earlier reported a 0.5 percentage point rise in its business confidence index to 113.7 in March, the highest level since October last year when it stood at 114.3.
Van Rensburg said there had been a positive response to Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's maiden budget which had steadied the rand and boosted financial markets.
The mood was particularly upbeat in the manufacturing sector where exporters have been given a fillip by a more competitive currency.

The physical volume of manufacturing production rose in March and manufacturers are confident about prospects. A Sacob survey found 74 perent of manufactuers expected higher sales volumes over the next 12 months and 71 percent expected to utilise more of their production capacity.

The non-agricultural sector of the economy should perform relatively well in 1997, but the overall level of growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 was likely to be only around 2.5 percent, down from the 3.1 percent recorded in 1996.
This reflected a lower contribution from agriculture, after last year's bumper harvests, reduced government expenditure and -- particularly -- continued high interest rates, van Rensbrug said.
Several factors were likely to mitigate against an cut in interest rates before the middle of the year, he said.

Firstly, money supply and credit extension growth remained well above the Reserve Bank's targets. Secondly, the central bank was likely to take a cautious stance before seeing the scale of outflow of funds following the next steps in the relaxation of exchange controls which take effect from July 1.

"Given that liberalisation of exchange controls could be associated with an outflow of capital, and that high interest rates are often used in an attempt to stem that flow, it is likely that interest rates will remain high at least until the third quarter."
South Africa's Bank rate currently stands at 17 percent and commercial banks' prime lending rate is 20.25 percent.

Van Rensburg said the 1996/97 budget was a key building block in the implementation of the government's much-praised macroeconomic strategy to double economic growth by 2000, but other elements still needed to be addressed.
Problem areas included lack of labour market flexiblity, public sector inefficiency and the government's inability to tackle crime.
Privatisation was also proceeding too slowly, despite last month's landmark deal to sell a 30 percent stake in Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium for $1.26 billion.
"The fact that there is now movement on privatisation is positive. But the speed and extent of the movement is still a little bit disappointing," van Rensburg said.
Privatisation offered the government an effective way to slash its debt, which currently totals 309.5 billion rand, or 55.3 percent of GDP.
